title: Malacca on the straits
hookLine: a sultanate on the straits, a hub of trade and learning

lines: A CITY NAMED FOR THE TREE.
cards: A prince on the run is resting under a tree by a river mouth. His hunting dogs are out in the brush. Suddenly they corner a mouse-deer, a tiny, delicate animal.

And the mouse-deer turns around and kicks one of the dogs straight into the river. The prince laughs, amazed. A place where even the smallest creature stands its ground, he says, is a good place for a city.
He asks the name of the tree he's sitting under. It's a melaka tree. That's how the Malay Annals tell the city's beginning.

teach.b: Malacca sat on a narrow sea lane between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra: the Straits of Malacca.

teach.h: THE WINDS MADE IT A PORT.
teach.b: And it had something no fort can build: the winds. The monsoon blows one way for part of the year and the other way for the rest.
Ships from India and Arabia came in on one wind, ships from China on the other, and both had to wait in port until the wind turned back. So Malacca became the place to wait, and to trade.
Its rulers took up Islam, and took the Arabic title sultan.

teach.h: A SULTAN, A DREAM, A SHIP.
teach.b: The Malay Annals tell this as a story too: the king dreams that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, teaches him the declaration of faith, and the next day a ship arrives carrying a scholar who leads the prayer, just as the dream foretold.
Whatever happened, Malacca became a center not only of trade but of learning. Scholars and Sufi teachers came.
The Malay language became a language of Islamic teaching and of commerce across the islands, written in an Arabic-based script called Jawi.
Merchants from many lands lived in their own quarters, with their own heads, and dealt in pepper, cloth, spices, porcelain and gold.
The Qur'an speaks of ships at sea as a sign: it says God made the sea of service, so ships could run on it and people could seek of His bounty, and give thanks.
Later, Portuguese ships came and took the city, and the sultans moved on. But the language, the script and the faith had already traveled.

how: In Malaysia, Malacca's history as a Muslim sultanate is taught as part of the country's story, and Malay is still written in Jawi script in some religious and traditional settings.

games.q: you rule Malacca. merchants from many lands crowd your harbor, each with their own customs. how do you house them?
o: let each community live in its own quarter, with its own head.
make every merchant live by one set of customs.

practice: Find the Straits of Malacca on a map, or picture a long, narrow channel of sea between two green coasts, and trace the water slowly from the open ocean at one end to the other: ships at anchor, languages on the docks, the call to prayer over the harbor.
If you pray, you can pray for travelers at sea.

wordCard.voice: Jawi. The Arabic-based script Malay took up in Malacca, the sultanate on the straits where trade and learning met. Today's word.

orig.note: Malay, from Arabic: Jawi, the Arabic-based script in which Malay became a language of Islamic teaching.
